title: Novo Nordisk's $725 Million Bet on Heart Inflammation Drug Fails in Major Trial
excerpt: Ziltivekimab did not reduce cardiovascular events in a 6,300-patient Phase 3 trial, sending shares down 9% and raising questions about the pharma giant's pipeline beyond obesity drugs.
body:
• Novo Nordisk's ziltivekimab failed its Phase 3 ZEUS trial, showing no significant reduction in major cardiovascular events
  • The drug, acquired through a $725 million buyout of Corvidia Therapeutics in 2020, targeted inflammation as a driver of heart disease
  • Novo's stock fell approximately 9% on the news, with analysts calling positive results from related studies now "highly unlikely"
  • The failure increases pressure on Novo to diversify its pipeline beyond blockbuster obesity and diabetes drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy

Novo Nordisk disclosed that ziltivekimab, its experimental anti-inflammatory drug targeting heart disease, failed to meet its primary endpoint in the Phase 3 ZEUS trial. The drug did not significantly reduce the risk of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACE) in patients with atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, chronic kidney disease, and elevated inflammation markers.

A Six-Year Bet That Didn't Pay Off

Novo acquired ziltivekimab in 2020 through its $725 million purchase of Corvidia Therapeutics, a deal that represented the Danish pharma giant's most ambitious push into cardiovascular medicine. The drug works by blocking interleukin-6, a protein linked to chronic inflammation that researchers believed was an independent driver of heart attacks and strokes.

The ZEUS trial enrolled approximately 6,300 patients across multiple countries and ran for several years. While the drug successfully reduced inflammatory biomarkers — confirming its mechanism of action — that biological effect did not translate into fewer heart attacks, strokes, or cardiovascular deaths.

"The hypothesis that targeting IL-6 alone would reduce cardiovascular events was always a high-risk proposition. The biology was compelling, but biology doesn't always predict clinical outcomes."

— BMO Capital Markets analyst note

Market Fallout and Pipeline Pressure

Novo's shares dropped roughly 9% following the announcement, erasing billions in market value. Analysts at BMO Capital Markets said the failure makes positive results from two other ongoing ziltivekimab studies "highly unlikely," effectively writing off the entire programme. Novo said it expects to record a non-cash impairment charge in the third quarter related to the Corvidia acquisition.

The failure comes at a sensitive time for Novo, which has been under investor scrutiny to demonstrate that its pipeline extends beyond GLP-1 drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy. Those obesity and diabetes blockbusters have powered Novo's market capitalisation to among the highest in global pharma, but concentration risk has been a persistent concern. Ziltivekimab was supposed to be a pillar of the company's cardiovascular strategy.

Why It Matters for South Asians

The trial's failure is particularly relevant for the Indian diaspora and South Asians globally, who face disproportionately high rates of cardiovascular disease, often developing heart conditions a decade earlier than other populations. The inflammation hypothesis — that chronic low-grade inflammation drives heart disease independently of cholesterol — had generated hope for a new class of treatments that could address the residual risk many patients face even when on statins.

The ZEUS result does not invalidate the inflammation theory entirely, but it narrows the therapeutic options. The CANTOS trial with canakinumab (a different anti-inflammatory) showed modest cardiovascular benefits years ago, but the drug was never approved for heart disease due to infection risks. Researchers will now reassess whether other inflammation pathways offer more promising targets.

What's Next

Novo said it will complete the analysis of the full ZEUS dataset and present results at a medical conference later this year. The company also reaffirmed its commitment to its GLP-1 pipeline, where it has multiple new formulations and indications in development. But for investors hoping Novo would evolve into a diversified cardiometabolic powerhouse, the ZEUS failure is a significant setback.
